\title{Modeling Lightning Strike Rate}
\author{Charlotte Uden}
\date{2024-11-30}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

This script uses the rethinking package to build Bayesian models of
lighting strike rate from eight climate variables. Two of these
variables are derived from information at various levels in the
atmosphere: CAPE (convective available potential energy) and CAPE x
Precipitation. These variables have been used before to model lighting
strike rate and provide a baseline for comparison with six surface level
climate variables: short wave radiation, relative humidity, temperature,
surface pressure, wind, and precipitation. The first model tested is a
null model, where lighting strike rate is modeled from a normal
distribution with no dependence on climate:

M0: Lightning Strike Rate \textasciitilde{} dnorm(mu, sigma) mu
\textasciitilde{} dnorm(0, 10) sigma \textasciitilde{} dexp(1)

The following eight models (M1 - M8) allow mu and sigma to change with
climate. Each climate variable is independently tested:

M1 - M8: Lightning Strike Rate \textasciitilde{} dnorm(mu, sigma) mu
\textless- a\_mu + b\_mu * climate\_variable\_x sigma \textless-
a\_sigma + b\_sigma * climate\_variable\_x a\_mu \textasciitilde{}
dnorm(0, 10) b\_mu \textasciitilde{} dnorm(0, 10) a\_sigma
\textasciitilde{} dexp(1) b\_sigma \textasciitilde{} dexp(1)

The compare() function is used to compare model performance,
specifically WAIC scores. The final ten models (M9 - M17) use the
performance of each of these single variable models to explore additive
affects and interaction terms.

\#M0: normal model, no dependance on climate

First, model lightning strike rate using the normal distribution with no
dependence on climate. Other models will be compared with this model.

sigma are dependant on climate: CAPE

sigma are dependant on climate: CAPE x Precipitation

WAIC scores: best score is m1, CAPE. followed by shortwave radiation and
temperature. (then CAPExPrecip, then relative humidity, wind, precip,
surface pressure, and the null model). \#M9: Short Wave Radiation +
Temperature

Lightning strike rate modeled from a normal distribution where mu and
sigma are dependant on climate: shortwave radiation and temperature,
where swr and temp have addative affects. They contribute independently
to the mean lightning strike rate and standard deviation. swr and temp
do not intereact; ie. the effect of swr on lighting is teh same
regardless of the temperature outside.

\#M10: Short Wave Radiation x Temperature

Lightning strike rate modeled from a normal distribution where mu and
sigma are dependent on climate: shortwave radiation and temperature,
which interact. The independent effects of short wave radiation and
temperature are not accounted for in this model.

\#M11: Short Wave Radiation + Temperature + (Short Wave Radiation x
Temperature)

Lightning strike rate modeled from a normal distribution where mu and
sigma are dependant on climate: shortwave radiation and temperature,
where swr and temp have addative affects and an interaction term.

Note taht d\_sigma is very close to 0, which make the interaction term
between swr and tair also almost 0 - so interactions between tair and
swr are minimal. This means that m11 is essentially the same as m9. Add,
in fact, has a similar WAIC score as m9.

\#M12: Short Wave Radiation + Temperature + Relative Humidity

Lightning strike rate modeled from a normal distribution where mu and
sigma are dependant on climate: shortwave radiation, temperature, and
relative humidity, where each predictor variable has an additive affect,
but do not interact. Relative humidity has been added since it has the
next best WAIC score when comparing simpler models that predict lighting
from just one climate variable.

  \AttributeTok{RH =}\NormalTok{ train}\SpecialCharTok{$}\NormalTok{rh)}

\#M13: Short Wave Radiation + Temperature + Relative Humidity + Wind

Lightning strike rate modeled from a normal distribution where mu and
sigma are dependent on climate: shortwave radiation, temperature,
relative humidity, and wind, where each predictor variable has an
additive affect, but do not interact. The wind model has the next best
WAIC score.

\#M14: Short Wave Radiation + Temperature + Relative Humidity + Wind +
Precipitation

Lightning strike rate modeled from a normal distribution where mu and
sigma are dependent on climate: shortwave radiation, temperature,
relative humidity, wind, and precipitation, where each predictor
variable has an additive affect, but do not interact. The precipitation
model has the next best WAIC score.

\#M15: Short Wave Radiation + Temperature + Relative Humidity + Wind +
Precipitation + Surface Pressure

Lightning strike rate modeled from a normal distribution where mu and
sigma are dependent on climate: shortwave radiation, temperature,
relative humidity, wind, precipitation, and surface pressure, where each
predictor variable has an additive affect, but do not interact. The
surface pressure model has the next best WAIC score, but also the lowest
after the null model, so it may not improve predictions by much.

\#M16: Short Wave Radiation + Temperature + Relative Humidity +
Precipitation + Surface Pressure

Adding surface pressure to the model produces a lower WAIC score, and
wind also reduces the WAIC score. The next two models remove wind, then
surface pressure and wind.
